sourceCopy.title: Discount Calculator — Sale Price, Savings & Stacks
sourceCopy.description: Find a sale price, reverse a discount or combine several offers. See exact savings and rounded amounts with clear steps. Free in your browser.
sourceCopy.heading: Discount Calculator
sourceCopy.intro: Check a sale price or find the discount from two prices. Combine offers without adding percentages that use different bases.

sourceCopy.examplesHeading: Four useful ways to get started

examples.heading: A straightforward offer
examples.text: 20% off 100 gives a sale price of 80.00 and savings of 20.00.

examples.heading: Check a claimed discount
examples.text: A price reduced from 80 to 60 is a 25% discount, with savings of 20.00.

examples.heading: Two successive offers
examples.text: 20% off, followed by 10% off, takes 100 to 72.00. The combined saving is 28%, not 30%.

examples.heading: Recover the original price
examples.text: A sale price of 72 after a 20% discount came from an original price of 90.00.

steps.heading: Choose the question
steps.text: Select the mode that matches your task. The input labels follow that choice.

steps.heading: Enter the values
steps.text: Use one currency for both prices. Enter percentage numbers without %. Stacked rates use commas between offers.

steps.heading: Check the result
steps.text: Calculate, inspect the working and save the result if needed. Cancel stops a long job.

method.heading: The method behind this result
paragraphs: Percent off uses sale price = original × (1 - rate/100). The savings are the difference between original and sale price. The original must be positive, and a discount rate lies from zero to one hundred percent.

Find the discount uses the original price and the actual sale price. The saved amount divided by the original gives the discount rate. A sale price above the original is an increase, so this discount mode rejects it rather than reporting negative savings.

Fixed amount off subtracts a stated coupon amount from the original. The reduction cannot exceed the original in this model. A coupon worth twenty off a price of ninety-five therefore gives seventy-five, independent of any percentage label.

Successive discounts apply one multiplier after another. Each percentage acts on the amount left by the previous offer. Multiplying 0.8 by 0.9 leaves 0.72 of the original. Adding the percentages would incorrectly treat both offers as reductions from the same base.

Recover original price divides the sale price by the remaining fraction. A one-hundred-percent discount leaves no information about the original, because every original could produce a free item. That case is rejected as undefined instead of guessed.

Calculations remain exact fractions until display. Amounts round to two decimal places, with half-cent ties away from zero. Exact final values are also shown. Tax, shipping, minimum-spend rules and store-specific coupon restrictions are not inferred.

uses.heading: Use the result with the right assumptions
paragraphs: Use the reverse mode to compare the actual starting and final prices behind an offer. It checks the arithmetic only. It does not verify a retailer’s claimed previous price or decide whether a promotion complies with local rules.

Use successive discounts when a store applies offers in sequence. Confirm the order and whether each offer is actually eligible. A percentage and a fixed coupon are different operations, so a store’s stated sequence still matters.

For an actual transaction, follow the shop’s item-level and tax rounding policy. The page uses a transparent arithmetic convention and shows the exact result before display rounding. Small differences can arise when several items are rounded separately.

privacy.heading: Private calculations, clear limits
paragraphs: Your inputs and results stay in this browser. Calculation runs in a local worker, without a calculation API or uploaded data.
The page saves only your theme preference. A copied link contains the selected inputs and options, so share it deliberately.
Large calculations depend on device time and memory. Cancel stops the active job. An error clears old answers and disables their downloads.

faq.question: Can I find the sale price from a percentage?
faq.answer: Yes. Choose Percent off, enter the original price and rate, then read the sale price and saved amount.

faq.question: Can I find the percentage from two prices?
faq.answer: Choose Find the discount. Enter a positive original price and a sale price from zero up to that original.

faq.question: Do two discounts add together?
faq.answer: Usually no. Successive discounts act on changing bases. Twenty percent followed by ten percent gives a 28% total reduction.

faq.question: Can I enter a fixed coupon?
faq.answer: Yes. Choose Fixed amount off. The coupon cannot exceed the original price in this calculation.

faq.question: How do I recover the original price?
faq.answer: Choose Recover original price and enter the sale price and known percentage reduction. A 100% reduction cannot determine the original.

faq.question: Does this include sales tax?
faq.answer: No. It calculates the entered prices before any tax or shipping rule you have not included yourself.

faq.question: Why does an exact value contain a fraction?
faq.answer: Decimal prices and percentages are calculated exactly. The money display rounds to two places, while the exact value preserves any remainder.

faq.question: How are half-cent ties rounded?
faq.answer: They round away from zero at the two-place money display. Store or invoice policies may use another convention.

faq.question: Can the sale price be higher than the original?
faq.answer: Not in the discount modes. Use percentage change when you want to describe a price increase.

faq.question: Is there a limit on stacked offers?
faq.answer: There is no fixed offer count. Separate the percentage numbers with commas; practical work is limited by device memory and time.
